mu-91348b5a.stem: Which smooth muscle raises the upper eyelid and is supplied by sympathetic fibres?
mu-91348b5a.explanation: Smooth muscle fibres separating from the underside of levator palpebrae superioris attach to the tarsal plate and are supplied by the sympathetic system. In Horner syndrome paralysis of this muscle causes a mild ptosis of 1–2 mm; complete ptosis suggests oculomotor palsy.
notes: It is striated muscle supplied by the oculomotor nerve.
It draws the eyebrows together; supplied by the facial nerve.
It wrinkles the forehead; supplied by the facial nerve.
It closes the eyelid; supplied by the facial nerve.

mu-53b19428.stem: Where does the upper head of lateral pterygoid attach?
options: Pterygoid tuberosity on the inner surface of the angle of the mandible
Articular disc and capsule of the temporomandibular joint
Outer surface of the ramus of the mandible
mu-53b19428.explanation: The upper head of lateral pterygoid attaches to the articular disc and capsule, the lower head to the pterygoid fovea on the neck of the mandible. On opening the mouth it pulls the condyle and disc forwards together towards the articular tubercle. Temporalis attaches to the coronoid process, medial pterygoid to the inner surface of the angle and masseter to its outer surface.
notes: This is the insertion of medial pterygoid.
This is the insertion of temporalis.
This is the origin of mylohyoid.
This is the insertion of masseter.

mu-1b6635d3.stem: Which muscle of mastication attaches to the inner surface of the angle of the mandible?
mu-1b6635d3.explanation: Medial pterygoid arises from the inner surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and attaches to the inner surface of the angle of the mandible (pterygoid tuberosity). With masseter it forms a 'sling' around the mandible from inside and outside and closes the jaw.

mu-617e6f31.stem: What is the insertion of temporalis?
options: Coronoid process of the mandible and anterior border of the ramus
mu-617e6f31.explanation: Temporalis arises fan-like from the whole temporal fossa, passes under the zygomatic arch and attaches to the coronoid process. Its anterior fibres close the jaw and its posterior horizontal fibres retract the mandible; it is supplied by the deep temporal branches of the mandibular nerve.

mu-e4dd7835.stem: Which is the main muscle that protrudes the tongue?
mu-e4dd7835.explanation: Genioglossus arises from the superior mental spine; its posterior fibres pull the root of the tongue forwards and protrude the tongue. In unilateral hypoglossal palsy the healthy genioglossus pushes the tongue across, so it deviates to the side of the lesion. Hyoglossus pulls the tongue down, styloglossus back and up.
notes: It pulls the tongue up and back.
It raises the root of the tongue; supplied by the vagus nerve.
It forms the floor of the mouth; it is not a tongue muscle.
It pulls the tongue down and back.

mu-9037320a.stem: Which of the following does NOT pass on the superficial (outer) surface of hyoglossus?
options: Vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve
mu-9037320a.explanation: Hyoglossus is an important landmark of the submandibular region: the hypoglossal nerve with its accompanying vein, the lingual nerve and the submandibular duct run on its surface, while the lingual artery passes deep (medial) to it. In surgery the lingual artery is therefore sought at the posterior border of the muscle.

mu-a4f34d20.stem: Where does the intermediate tendon joining the two bellies of digastric attach?
options: To the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
To the digastric fossa of the mandible
To the mastoid notch of the mastoid process
By a fibrous loop to the body and greater horn of the hyoid bone
mu-a4f34d20.explanation: The anterior belly arises from the digastric fossa and the posterior belly from the mastoid notch; the intermediate tendon is bound to the hyoid by a fibrous sling and passes between the split tendon of stylohyoid. The anterior belly is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid (V3), the posterior belly by the facial nerve.
notes: This is the attachment of sternothyroid and thyrohyoid.
This is the origin of the anterior belly.
This is the origin of stylohyoid and styloglossus.
This is the origin of the posterior belly.

mu-3b03b92e.stem: Which muscle forms the floor of the mouth (oral diaphragm)?
mu-3b03b92e.explanation: The two mylohyoid muscles arise from the mylohyoid lines of the mandible and meet at the midline raphe and the body of the hyoid, forming the floor of the mouth. The superficial and deep parts of the submandibular gland curve around the posterior border of this muscle.

mu-2c22e054.stem: What holds the intermediate tendon of omohyoid in place?
options: The greater horn of the hyoid bone
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
The back of the manubrium of the sternum
A fascial sling attached to the clavicle and 1st rib
mu-2c22e054.explanation: The inferior belly of omohyoid arises from the upper border of the scapula (near the suprascapular notch), the superior belly from the body of the hyoid. The two bellies meet in front of the internal jugular vein at the intermediate tendon, which is held to the clavicle and 1st rib by a sling of deep cervical fascia.

mu-84400e81.stem: Into which two smaller triangles does the inferior belly of omohyoid divide the posterior triangle of the neck?
mu-84400e81.explanation: The posterior triangle (between SCM, trapezius and clavicle) is divided by the inferior belly of omohyoid into the occipital triangle above and the omoclavicular (supraclavicular) triangle below. The accessory nerve crosses the occipital triangle; the third part of the subclavian artery and the trunks of the brachial plexus lie in the omoclavicular triangle.

mu-8462ad75.stem: Which muscles bound the carotid triangle?
options: The two bellies of digastric and the mandible
Anterior belly of digastric, hyoid bone and the midline of the neck
Sternocleidomastoid, superior belly of omohyoid and the midline of the neck
Sternocleidomastoid, superior belly of omohyoid and posterior belly of digastric
mu-8462ad75.explanation: The carotid triangle contains the bifurcation of the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein, the vagus nerve and the hypoglossal nerve. The other options are, respectively, the boundaries of the submandibular, submental, posterior and muscular triangles.

mu-4c566931.stem: Where do the two heads of sternocleidomastoid arise?
options: Manubrium of the sternum and 1st costal cartilage
Front of the manubrium of the sternum and medial 1/3 of the clavicle
Lateral 1/3 of the clavicle and acromion
Mastoid process and superior nuchal line
Body of the sternum and xiphoid process
mu-4c566931.explanation: The sternal head arises from the front of the manubrium and the clavicular head from the medial third of the clavicle; the muscle attaches to the mastoid process and lateral half of the superior nuchal line. The small triangular hollow between the two heads (lesser supraclavicular fossa) lies over the internal jugular vein.

mu-0ce01850.stem: What is the insertion of scalenus anterior?
options: Behind the groove for the subclavian artery on the 1st rib
mu-0ce01850.explanation: Scalenus anterior arises from the anterior tubercles of the C3–C6 transverse processes and attaches to the scalene tubercle of the 1st rib. The subclavian vein passes in front of this tubercle and the subclavian artery in the groove behind it. Scalenus medius attaches to the 1st rib behind the groove, scalenus posterior to the 2nd rib.
notes: This is the insertion of subclavius.
Scalenus anterior never attaches to C7.
This is the insertion of scalenus medius.
This is the insertion of scalenus posterior.

mu-8af04076.stem: Which laryngeal muscle tenses the vocal folds and is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve?
mu-8af04076.explanation: Cricothyroid tilts the thyroid cartilage forwards and downwards, lengthening and tensing the vocal folds; it is important for high notes. It is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle on the outer surface of the larynx and is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; all the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
